transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Hello, Easy Life Cleaning Services, Jacinta speaking.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Oh hello. I'm looking for a cleaning service for my apartment – do you do domestic cleaning?

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Well, it's just a one-bedroom flat. Do you have a basic cleaning package?

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Yes. For a one-bedroom flat we're probably looking at about two hours for a clean. So we'd do a thorough clean of all surfaces in each room, and polish them where necessary. Does your apartment have carpets?

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: No, I don't have any, but <q id="1">the floor would need cleaning</q>.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Of course – <q id="1">we'd do that in every room</q>. And we'd do a thorough clean of the kitchen and bathroom.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Then we have some additional services which you can request if you want – so for example, we can clean your oven for you every week.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Actually, I hardly ever use that, but <q id="2">can you do the fridge?</q>

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Sure. Would you like that done every week?

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. And would ironing clothes be an additional service you can do?

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Yes, of course.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: It wouldn't be much, <q id="3">just my shirts for work that week</q>.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: That's fine. And we could also clean your microwave if you want.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: No, I wipe that out pretty regularly so there's no need for that.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: We also offer additional services that you might want a bit less often, say every month. So for example, if <q id="4">the inside of your windows need cleaning</q>, we could do that.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Yes, that'd be good. I'm on the fifteenth floor, so the outside gets done regularly by specialists, but the inside does get a bit grubby.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: And we could arrange for your curtains to get cleaned if necessary.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: No, they're OK. But <q id="5">would you be able to do something about the balcony?</q> It's quite small and I don't use it much, but it could do with a wash every month or so.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Yes, we can get the pressure washer onto that.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Now if you're interested, we do offer some other possibilities to do with general maintenance. For example, if you have a problem with water and you need a plumber in a hurry, we can put you in touch with a reliable one who can come out straightaway. <q id="6">And the same thing if you need an electrician.</q>

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Right. That's good to know. I've only just moved here so I don't have any of those sorts of contacts.

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: And I don't know if this is of interest to you, but we also offer a special vacuum cleaning system which can improve the indoor air quality of your home by <q id="7">capturing up to 99% of all the dust in the air. So if you're troubled by allergies, this can make a big difference.</q>

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Right. In fact, I don't have that sort of problem, but I'll bear it in mind. Now can you tell me a bit about your cleaning staff?

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Of course. So all our cleaners are very carefully selected. When they apply to us, they have to <q id="8">undergo a security check with the police</q> to make sure they don't have any sort of criminal background, and, of course, they have to provide references as well. Then if we think they might be suitable for the job, <q id="9">we give them training for it. That lasts for two weeks</q> so it's very thorough, and at the end of it, they have a test. If they pass that, we take them on, but we monitor them very carefully – we ask <q id="10">all our clients to complete a review of their performance after every visit and to email it to us.</q> So we can pick up any problems straightaway and deal with them.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: OK, well that all sounds good. And will I always have the same cleaner?

transcript.speaker: JACINTA
transcript.text: Yes, we do our best to organise it that way, and we usually manage it.

transcript.speaker: CLIENT
transcript.text: Good. That's fine. Right, so I'd like to go ahead and ...

As many of you here today have worked in the hotel industry for some time, I'm sure you have experienced the problem of high staff turnover in your hotels. Every hotel relies on having loyal and experienced members of staff who make sure that everything runs smoothly. If staff are constantly changing, it can make life difficult for everyone. But why do staff leave frequently in many hotels? Of course, many hotel jobs, such as cleaning, are low-skilled and are not well-paid. A lot of managers think it's this and the long hours that are the main causes of high staff turnover – but what they don't realise is that <q id="11">it's the lack of training in many hotel jobs which is a huge factor.</q>

So, what kind of problems does a high turnover of staff cause? Well, <q id="12">having to recruit new staff all the time can be very time-consuming, and managers may have to cover some duties while waiting for new staff to arrive.</q> This means they don't have time to think about less immediate problems such as how to improve their service. When staff leave, it can also severely affect the colleagues they leave behind. It has a negative effect on remaining staff, who may start to feel that they too should be thinking about leaving.

So, what can be done to change this situation? Firstly, managers should stop making basic errors which leave their staff feeling upset and resentful. When organising shifts, for example, <q id="13">make sure you never give certain staff preferential treatment. All staff should be given some choice about when they work</q>, and everyone should have to work some evening and weekend shifts. If you treat staff fairly, they'll be more likely to step in and help when extra staff are needed.

Keeping staff happy has other tangible benefits for the business. Take the Dunwich Hotel as an example. It had been experiencing a problem with staff complaints and in order to deal with this, invested in staff training and improved staff conditions. Not only did the level of complaints fall, but <q id="14">they also noticed a significant increase in the amount each customer spent during their stay.</q> They have now introduced a customer loyalty scheme which is going really well.
Now I'd like to look at some ways you can reduce staff turnover in your hotels, and I'll do this by giving some examples of hotels where I've done some training recently.

The Sun Club received feedback which showed that staff thought managers didn't value their opinions. They weren't <q id="15">made to feel they were partners who were contributing to the success of the business as a whole. This situation has changed. Junior staff at all levels are regularly invited to meetings where their ideas are welcomed.</q>

A year ago, The Portland recognised the need to invest in staff retention. <q id="16">Their first step was to introduce a scheme for recognising talent amongst their employees.</q> The hope is that <q id="16">organising training for individuals with management potential</q> will encourage them to stay with the business.

At Bluewater, managers decided to recognise 50 high achievers from across the company's huge hotel chain. <q id="17">As a reward, they're sent on an all-expenses-paid trip abroad</q> every year. Fun is an important element in the trips, but there's also the opportunity to learn something useful. This year's trip included a visit to a brewery, where staff learned about the new beer that would be served in the hotel.

Pentlow Hotels identified that retention of junior reception staff was an issue. <q id="18">In order to encourage them to see that working in a hotel could be worthwhile and rewarding, with good prospects, they introduced a management programme.</q> These staff were given additional responsibilities and the chance to work in various roles in the hotel.

Green Planet wanted to be seen as a caring employer. To make life easier for staff, many of whom had childcare responsibilities, the hotel began <q id="19">issuing vouchers to help cover the cost of childcare.</q>

Louise Marsh at The Amesbury has one of the best staff retention rates in the business. Since she joined the company, she has made a huge effort to achieve this by <q id="20">creating a co-operative and supportive environment. For her, the staff are part of a large family where everyone is valued.</q>
OK, now I'd like to ...

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Hi Thomas, how are you enjoying the course so far?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah, I think it's good.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Remind me – why did you decide to study sports science? Didn't you want to be a professional athlete when you were at school?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah – that was my goal, and <q id="21">all my classmates assumed I would achieve it; they thought I was brilliant.</q>

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: That must have been a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Mm, I thought I could win anything. There was no one who could run faster than me.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Exactly – so what happened? Did your mum and dad want you to be more 'academic'?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Not at all. <q id="22">Perhaps they should have pushed me harder, though.</q>

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: <q id="22">I think I should have practised more.</q>

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: What makes you say that?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Well, I went out to Kenya for a couple of weeks to train ...

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Really! I didn't know that.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: I was chosen to go there out of loads of kids and run with some of the top teenage athletes in the world. And ... I was so calm about it. <q id="23">I just kept thinking how fortunate I was. What a great chance this was!</q> Everyone back home was so proud of me. But once we started competing, I very quickly realised I wasn't good enough.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: That must have been a huge shock.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: <q id="24">I thought 'this can't be happening'!</q> I was used to winning.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: I'm sorry to hear that.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: It's OK. I'm over it now and I think it's much better to do a university course and this one has such a variety of sports-related areas. It's going to be good.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Oh, I agree – I chose it because of that.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: So Jeanne – have you thought of any ideas for the discussion session next week on technology and sport?

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: We have to cover more than one sport, don't we?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: You know – we always think technology is about the future, but we could gather some ideas about past developments in sport.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Look at early types of equipment perhaps? Uh, I remember reading something about table tennis bats once – how they ended up being covered with pimpled rubber.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Cos they were just wooden at first, I'd imagine.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah. In about the 1920s, <q id="25">a factory was making rolls of the rubber in bulk</q> for something like horse harnesses.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Really!

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah – and <q id="25">someone realised that it'd make a perfect covering for the wooden bats.</q> So what about cricket – that's had a few innovative changes. Maybe the pads they wear on their legs?

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: I don't think they've changed much but, I'm just looking on the internet ... and it says that <q id="26">when the first cricket helmet came in, in 1978, the Australian batsman who first wore it was booed and jeered by people</q> watching because it was so ugly!

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Wow, players have to protect themselves from getting hurt! I mean everyone wears one now.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Mm, unlike the cycle helmet.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Well, unless you're a professional, but you're right, many ordinary bikers don't wear a helmet.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Hey, look at these pictures of original helmet designs. This one looks like an upside-down bowl!

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Yet, the woman's laughing – she's so proud to be wearing it!

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: It says <q id="27">serious cyclists ended up with wet hair</q> from all the hard exercise.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: I guess <q id="27">that's why they have large air vents in them now so that the skin can breathe more easily.</q>

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: OK, so we've done helmets. What about golf balls or better still golf clubs – they've changed a lot.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Yeah – I remember my great grandfather telling me that <q id="28">because a club was made entirely of wood, it would easily break and players had to get another.</q>

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: There's no wood at all in them now, is there?

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: No – they're much more powerful.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: The same must be true of hockey sticks.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: I don't think so because players still use wooden sticks today. What it does say here, though, is that <q id="29">when the game started you had to produce a stick yourself.</q>

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: I guess they just weren't being manufactured. So, one more perhaps. What about football?

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Well, I know the first balls were made of animal skin.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah, they covered them with pieces of leather that were stitched together, but ... the balls let in water when it rained.

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: Oh, that would have made them much heavier.

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: That's right. <q id="30">You can imagine the damage to players' necks when the ball was headed.</q>

transcript.speaker: JEANNE
transcript.text: How painful that must have been!

transcript.speaker: THOMAS
transcript.text: Yeah, well, I think we can put together some useful ideas ...

Hello everyone. Today we're going to look at another natural food product and that's maple syrup. What is this exactly? Well, maple syrup looks rather like clear honey, but it's not made by bees; it's produced from the plant fluid – or sap – inside the maple tree and that makes maple syrup a very natural product. <q id="31">Maple syrup is a thick, golden</q>, sweet-tasting liquid that can be bought in bottles or jars and poured onto food such as waffles and ice cream or used in the baking of cakes and pastries. It contains no preservatives or added ingredients, and <q id="32">it provides a healthy alternative to refined sugar.</q>

Let's just talk a bit about the maple tree itself, which is where maple syrup comes from. So, there are many species of maple tree, and they'll grow without fertilizer in areas where there's plenty of moisture in the soil. However, they'll only do this if another important criterion is fulfilled, which is that they must have full or partial sun exposure during the day and very cool nights – and I'll talk more about that in a minute. There are only certain parts of the world that provide all these conditions: one is Canada, and by that, I mean all parts of Canada, and the other is the north-eastern states of North America. <q id="33">In these areas, the climate suits the trees perfectly.</q> In fact, Canada produces over two-thirds of the world's maple syrup, which is why the five-pointed maple leaf is a Canadian symbol and has featured on the flag since 1964.

So how did maple syrup production begin? Well, long before Europeans settled in these parts of the world, the indigenous communities had started producing maple sugar. They bored holes in the trunks of maple trees and used containers made of tree bark to collect the liquid sap as it poured out. As they were unable to keep the liquid for any length of time – they didn't have storage facilities in those days – they boiled the liquid by <q id="34">placing pieces of rock that had become scorching hot from the sun into the sap.</q> They did this until it turned into sugar, and they were then able to use this to sweeten their food and drinks. Since that time, improvements have been made to the process, but it has changed very little overall.

So let's look at the production of maple syrup today. Clearly, the maple forests are a valuable resource in many Canadian and North American communities. The trees have to be well looked after and <q id="35">they cannot be used to make syrup until the trunks reach a diameter of around 25 centimetres. This can take anything up to 40 years.</q> As I've already mentioned, maple trees need the right conditions to grow and also to produce sap. Why is this? Well, what happens is that during a cold night, the tree absorbs water from the soil, and that rises through the tree's vascular system. But then in the warmer daytime, the change in temperature causes the water to be pushed back down to the bottom of the tree. This continual movement – up and down – leads to the formation of the sap needed for maple syrup production.

When the tree is ready, it can be tapped <q id="36">and this involves drilling a small hole into the trunk and inserting a tube into it that ends in a bucket.</q> The trees can often take several taps, though the workers take care not to cause any damage to the healthy growth of the tree itself. The sap that comes out of the trees consists of 98 percent water and 2 percent sugar and other nutrients. It has to be boiled so that much of that water evaporates, and this process has to take place immediately, using what are called evaporators. <q id="37">These are basically extremely large pans – the sap is poured into these, a fire is built and the pans are then heated until the sap boils.</q> As it does this, the water evaporates, and the syrup begins to form. <q id="38">The evaporation process creates large quantities of steam</q>, and the sap becomes thicker and denser, and, at just the right moment, when the sap is thick enough to be called maple syrup, the worker removes it from the heat. After this process, something called <q id="39">'sugar sand' has to be filtered out as this builds up during the boiling and gives the syrup a cloudy appearance</q> and a slightly gritty taste. Once this has been done, the syrup is ready to be packaged so that it can be used for a whole variety of products. <q id="40">It takes 40 litres of sap to produce one litre of maple syrup</q> so you can get an idea of how much is needed!
So that's the basic process. In places like Quebec where ...
